parvenu

parvenu runs common R work on all your cores, in Rust. It has two families of functions:

  • Base R functions with base R’s results: match(), %in%, duplicated(), unique(), findInterval(), factor(), table(), the set operations, as.Date(), as.POSIXct(), rank(), rowsum(), and approx(), plus row matching on several key columns.
  • Text search: regex detection, counting, location, extraction, and replacement. Also dictionary lookup and replacement of many terms at once.

par_match(), %par_in%, par_duplicated(), par_unique(), par_any_duplicated(), par_union(), par_intersect(), par_setdiff(), par_factor(), par_table(), par_find_interval(), and the functions under Dates, ranks, and sums behave exactly like base R, so they are drop-in replacements. par_detect() is grepl() with the syntax of Rust’s regex crate, which never backtracks.

The gains are largest where base R is slow and the work is bound by CPU: matching text against a large dictionary of terms, and looking up millions of keys.

When the wait matters

Many single calls take base R a second or less, even on millions of elements. A second is a fine wait. It grows longer in three ways: two sizes multiply, such as strings and terms; the input runs to tens of millions; or a call repeats, on every keystroke or in every resample. Some cases, on 8 cores (bench/at-scale.R and the other scripts in bench/):

Case Base R parvenu
10,000 terms in 100,000 strings 38s 4.3ms
A capture group from each of 1 million strings 18s 0.21s
Every match in 1 million strings 11s 0.21s
Counting matches in 1 million strings 8.7s 20ms
10 million times from web server logs 53s 0.48s
10 million times with milliseconds 2.6 min 0.21s
A search box over 10 million rows, per keystroke 0.40s 39ms
Spearman’s correlation in 1,000 bootstrap resamples of 200,000 rows 1.6 min 18s
  • Large dictionaries. Medical vocabularies, gene names, and place names run to tens of thousands of terms. Base R’s regex engines refuse an alternation that long: PCRE stops near 3,400 terms of 8 letters. What’s left is a loop over the terms, here with grepl(fixed = TRUE). stringi takes an alternation of 10,000 terms, but needs 43s. Both grow with strings times terms, so a corpus of a million abstracts takes them minutes.
  • Regexes that return more than TRUE or FALSE. regmatches() on regexec() or gregexpr() takes 9-18s per million strings, stringi 0.2-5s, and parvenu 0.02-0.21s.
  • Many times. A month of logs from a site that serves a few requests a second holds 10 million times such as "07/Nov/2026:21:43:00 +0000", read with format = "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z". Such times repeat within a second, so parsing only unique() times and matching them back brings base R down to 17s. Times with milliseconds, as from sensors or event streams, don’t repeat. Given format, base R takes 1.3 minutes for them instead of 2.6. data.table::fread() and readr parse ISO dates as they read. So this concerns times that reach R as text: other formats, or times extracted from log lines.
  • Interactive search. A Shiny filter searches again on every keystroke, and a response feels instant only within about a tenth of a second. Half a second is fine for one search, but as a lag after every key it makes the app feel sluggish. Case-insensitive search takes 0.66s in base R and 57ms in parvenu.
  • Resampling. A bootstrap of Spearman’s correlation ranks both columns in each resample. data.table::frank() takes 28s for the same.

Dictionary matching

Which of 100,000 strings mention any of 1,000 terms? A backtracking engine tries each term at each position. par_detect() compiles the alternation once into an automaton that finds all terms in one pass. It splits the strings across threads.

library(parvenu)

texts <- c("flights to new york", "a walk in yorkshire", "rain in paris", "a quiet day")
par_detect(texts, "york|paris")
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

Timed on 100,000 strings and 1,000 terms, against base R and stringi:

Show code 
set.seed(1)

word <- function(n) {
  vapply(
    seq_len(n),
    function(i) paste(sample(letters, 8, TRUE), collapse = ""),
    ""
  )
}

vocabulary <- word(1e4)

x <- paste(
  sample(vocabulary, 1e5, TRUE),
  sample(vocabulary, 1e5, TRUE),
  sample(999, 1e5, TRUE)
)

terms <- sample(vocabulary, 1000)
pattern <- paste(terms, collapse = "|")
results <- bench::mark(
  base = grepl(pattern, x, perl = TRUE),
  stringi = stringi::stri_detect_regex(x, pattern),
  parvenu = par_detect(x, pattern),
  iterations = 10
)
results[, c("expression", "median")]
plot(results)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   expression   median
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm>
#> 1 base          14.9s
#> 2 stringi        8.2s
#> 3 parvenu      19.7ms

Wrap the alternation in \b( and )\b to match whole words only, or use par_match_term(whole_word = TRUE) below. Terms that contain regex metacharacters such as . or ( need a backslash in front of them. Avoid (?i) in front of a large alternation: it defeats the optimization above, and the same search takes over a hundred times longer. For a case-insensitive search, use par_match_term() below, or lowercase both the strings and the terms.

Which term?

par_match_term() finds which term each string contains, as a position in terms. It is match() for substrings. If a string contains several terms, the one earliest in terms wins. So put specific terms such as "new york" before general ones such as "york". The terms are literal, so they need no escaping. ignore_case = TRUE ignores case in any script, at full speed for ASCII text. whole_word = TRUE skips hits inside longer words, so "york" matches "york, uk" but not "yorkshire". whole_word = "start" matches prefixes, such as "happ" in "happiness".

places <- c("new york", "york", "paris")
par_match_term(texts, places)
#> [1]  1  2  3 NA
par_match_term(texts, places, whole_word = TRUE)
#> [1]  1 NA  3 NA

Timed on the same data, against a stringi search per term:

Show code 
# The same result with stringi: one search per term
stringi_loop <- function(x, terms) {
  out <- rep(NA_integer_, length(x))
  for (i in rev(seq_along(terms))) {
    out[stringi::stri_detect_fixed(x, terms[i])] <- i
  }
  out
}

upper <- toupper(x)

results <- bench::mark(
  stringi = stringi_loop(x, terms),
  `parvenu (default)` = par_match_term(x, terms),
  `parvenu (ignore case)` = par_match_term(upper, terms, ignore_case = TRUE),
  iterations = 10,
  filter_gc = FALSE
)
results[, c("expression", "median")]
plot(results)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   expression              median
#>   <bch:expr>            <bch:tm>
#> 1 stringi                  4.96s
#> 2 parvenu (default)       2.55ms
#> 3 parvenu (ignore case)    2.6ms

par_count_term() counts the hits of the terms in each string. With weights, it sums their scores, as for scoring text against a sentiment lexicon. par_which_term() finds every term each string contains, for tagging. par_replace_term() replaces each term with its replacement: 1,000 terms in 100,000 strings take 21ms, where stringi’s stri_replace_all_fixed(vectorize_all = FALSE) takes 3.7s. With fixed = FALSE, the terms of all four _term functions are regexes, searched in one pass. That is slower than literal terms, but several times faster than one par_detect() per term.

General matching

Show code 
keys <- sample.int(1e8, size = 1e6)
x <- sample.int(1e8, size = 1e7, replace = TRUE)

results <- bench::mark(
  base = match(x, keys),
  collapse = collapse::fmatch(x, keys),
  parvenu = par_match(x, keys),
  iterations = 10,
  filter_gc = FALSE
)
results[, c("expression", "median")]
plot(results)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   expression   median
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm>
#> 1 base        251.6ms
#> 2 collapse    179.6ms
#> 3 parvenu      14.4ms

par_match() handles integer, double, character, Date, and POSIXct vectors, and factors by their levels. Other classes, and inputs below 10,000 elements, go to base match(). %par_in% replaces %in%, and par_in() is the same as a regular function.

Both sides are hashed in parallel, so a join-like lookup of 10 million keys into 10 million others takes 0.1 seconds for integers and 0.2 for strings. The numbers behind the comparison with collapse are in bench/.

par_duplicated() returns the same as duplicated(), using the same parallel hash tables. Like base, it compares the rows of data frames. par_unique() returns the same as unique() and collects the first occurrences in the same pass. par_match_rows() matches rows on several key columns at once, as in a join. It hashes whole rows in parallel, so a lookup of 10 million rows into 10 million others takes a fraction of a second. Pasting the columns into strings for match() takes seconds per million.

par_find_interval() bins values by sorted breaks, such as ages into age groups. It returns the same as findInterval() under a clearer name, with a binary search per element on all cores. 10 million values into 10,000 breaks take a few dozen milliseconds, where base takes almost a second.

Single calls

Timed on 8 cores, against base R (the sections above and bench/ have the details, and comparisons with collapse, stringi, and data.table):

Function Replaces Task Time Base R Speedup
par_match_term() regexpr(perl = TRUE) on an alternation 1,000 terms in 100,000 strings 2.7ms 15s 5500x
par_detect() grepl(perl = TRUE) a regex in 1 million strings 17ms 0.25s 15x
par_match() match() 10 million strings in 10,000 keys 11ms 0.25s 23x
par_match() match() 10 million integers in 10,000 keys 8ms 0.12s 15x
par_match_rows() match() on pasted columns 1 million rows on two key columns 18ms 2.5s 134x
par_duplicated() duplicated() 10 million integers 42ms 0.49s 12x
par_unique() unique() 10 million integers 51ms 0.57s 11x
par_find_interval() findInterval() 10 million values into 10,000 breaks 34ms 0.92s 27x

Dates, ranks, and sums

Some of base R’s slowest functions are not about matching at all. These return the same results, to the last bit. They fall back to base R for what they don’t cover. At a million dates or ten million numbers, on 8 cores:

Function Replaces Task Time Base R Speedup
par_as_date() as.Date() 1 million dates 7ms 4.6s 657x
par_as_posixct(tz = "UTC") as.POSIXct(tz = "UTC") 1 million times 12ms 15s 1250x
par_rank() rank() 10 million doubles 0.24s 9.8s 41x
par_rowsum() rowsum() 10 million values in 100,000 groups 0.1s 1.2s 12x
par_approx() approx() 10 million points into 10,000 0.1s 0.63s 6x

par_as_posixct() parses in Rust in any time zone. Outside UTC, base R’s C code places the times, so 1 million take 0.83s over two years, or 2.1s over 127 years, instead of 12ms (base: 37s). par_rank() beats data.table::frank() (0.61s), while collapse sums groups faster than par_rowsum() (67ms).

Use cases

The use-cases article shows each function at work: coding free text with a keyword table, scoring text against a lexicon, filtering logs, validating identifiers, extracting and rewriting parts of strings, lookups and joins on one or several keys, finding duplicates, and binning. The performance article collects ways to keep calls fast, such as keeping repeated values as a factor, and the inputs that take a slow path.

Threads

The default is all cores, or the RAYON_NUM_THREADS environment variable. Every function takes nthreads, and options(parvenu.threads = 2) sets the default for a session. Inputs too small to keep that many threads busy use fewer.

parvenu and process pools

mizu and mirai run any R code in parallel, on pools of R processes. mori shares R objects with such processes without copying them. parvenu is narrower: it has its own multithreaded versions of particular functions. Use the pools for model fits, bootstraps, and any other R code that parvenu doesn’t cover. For the functions it does cover, a single parvenu call is much faster than splitting the input across workers that each call base R. Each worker still runs base R’s code on one core. Also, the input has to reach the workers, and the results have to come back. On 8 cores, with the pools already started (bench/process-pools.R):

Task Base R mizu mirai mirai + mori parvenu
grepl(perl = TRUE) on 1 million strings 0.25s 0.58s 0.15s 0.15s 10ms
match() of 10 million integers into 1 million keys 0.25s 0.62s 0.37s 0.29s 15ms
as.Date() on 1 million strings 4.6s 1.2s 0.99s 0.96s 7ms

On one thread, parvenu takes 56ms, 71ms, and 33ms for these tasks. So most of its lead over base R comes from its own code rather than from threads: a regex engine that doesn’t backtrack, a faster hash table, and a parser for the common date formats.

Regex syntax

Most patterns mean the same in Rust’s regex crate and in PCRE. The differences:

  • No backreferences or lookaround. In return, matching time grows only linearly with the string.
  • \d, \w, and \s match Unicode by default. Write [0-9] or (?-u:\d) for ASCII.
  • Flags go in the pattern: (?i) ignores case.
  • NA returns NA, where grepl() returns FALSE.

For example:

grepl("(a)\\1", "aa")      # TRUE
par_detect("aa", "(a)\\1") # error: backreferences are not supported

grepl("\\d", "٣", perl = TRUE) # FALSE: an Arabic-Indic three
par_detect("٣", "\\d")         # TRUE

grepl("b", "ABC", ignore.case = TRUE) # TRUE
par_detect("ABC", "(?i)b")            # TRUE

grepl("a", NA)      # FALSE
par_detect(NA, "a") # NA

fixed = TRUE finds pattern as it is, as in grepl(fixed = TRUE). pattern can also have one element per string, as in stringi.

par_extract() returns the first match in each string, or a capture group of it, which takes the place of lookaround. par_extract_all() returns every match. par_locate() finds where the first match starts and ends, as regexpr() does. par_replace() replaces the first match, as sub() does. par_replace_all() replaces every match, as gsub() does. Both use $1 instead of \\1 for a group. Only R’s own thread can make R strings, so the more strings change, the longer that takes. Where a tenth of a million strings change, it is about 6 times faster than gsub(perl = TRUE). Where all of them change, it is about twice as fast.

Installation

When parvenu is on CRAN, you will be able to install it as usual:

install.packages("parvenu")

The development version requires the Rust toolchain. When Rust is installed, run:

pak::pak("lhdjung/parvenu")
# or devtools::install_github("lhdjung/parvenu")
